# What Is a Restricted Category in Advertising?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-restricted-category/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-04-14 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Distribution

> Summary: Ad platforms sort products into prohibited, restricted and open groups, using a process built to refuse a legitimate business rather than approve a harmful one. Google, Meta, TikTok and Apple each publish the conditions, and they change them often. A restricted classification is a map of where to build distribution, not a review to argue with or evade.

A restricted category is a group of products an ad platform will advertise only with conditions, such as prior approval, proof of licensing, certification, geographic limits, age limits or required disclaimers. Platforms sort every product into prohibited, restricted or open, using a process built to prefer refusing a legitimate business over approving a harmful one. Financial services, crypto, health, gambling and alcohol are restricted on most platforms, with rules that differ by country and change several times a year. Treat the classification as a map of where to build, not as a review to argue with.

Every major advertising platform maintains a policy that sorts products into three groups: those it will run without question, those it will run with conditions, and those it will not run at all. The middle group is what the industry calls restricted categories, and it is larger than most founders expect until they are in it.

## The three groups

**Prohibited.** Products the platform will not advertise under any conditions. The list varies but typically includes weapons, illegal products, counterfeit goods, certain adult content and, on some platforms and in some geographies, entire financial or health sub-categories. No documentation changes the answer. Google disapproves ads for binary options and credit repair services, and bans ads for initial coin offerings and DeFi trading protocols regardless of location.

**Restricted.** Products the platform will advertise only with conditions: prior written approval, proof of licensing or registration, certification, geographic limits, age restrictions, specific disclaimers or limits on claims. Financial services, cryptocurrency, gambling, alcohol, pharmaceuticals, health and supplements, dating, political content and several others sit here on most platforms, with the exact rules differing by platform and country.

**Open.** Everything else, subject to the general policies on claims, creative and landing pages that apply to all advertisers.

## What the conditions look like on four platforms

The conditions are not secret. They are published, and they are more mechanical than most rejection emails suggest.

| Platform | Financial services | Crypto | Health |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Google Ads | Verification required in some locations, with licences and registration numbers; physical address and fees must be disclosed | Exchanges and software wallets need approval and local registration, such as FCA registration in the UK or MiCA authorisation in the EU; DeFi protocols and ICOs banned | Online pharmacies, prescription drug services and addiction services need certification; prescription opioid ads banned with limited exceptions |
| Meta | US financial ads must run in a special ad category: fixed age range, no gender targeting, no lookalike audiences | Permission, or one of Meta's accepted regulatory licences, which Meta expanded from three to 27 in December 2021 | Not reviewed here |
| TikTok | Local licensing, disclosures and 18+ targeting in most markets | Prohibited in some markets; permitted with licensing and an application through a sales representative in others | Not reviewed here |
| Apple App Store | Apps in banking and financial services must be submitted by the legal entity providing the service | Exchanges only in countries where the app holds the licences; ICO and crypto futures apps only from approved financial institutions | Healthcare apps must be submitted by the legal entity providing the service |

*Policies checked on each platform's own pages on 16 November 2026, except where noted.*

Two patterns stand out. First, most conditions are about documents and geography, not about the product's quality. Second, the rules move. Google posted crypto policy updates in July 2025 for Canada, September 2025 for Argentina and February 2026 for Indonesia, each opening exchange and wallet advertising under local licensing. In June 2026 it announced financial services verification for 24 more European markets, with rolling enforcement from 23 July 2026. A restricted classification is a fact with a date on it.

## How the decision is made

The platform's policy is written by its legal, trust-and-safety and policy teams, and it is applied by a combination of automated classifiers and human reviewers who see the ad, the landing page, the account history and sometimes the business documents, but never the product in use.

That last point explains most of the frustration. A reviewer is asked to decide quickly whether an account looks like a category that has caused the platform legal or reputational problems before. A legitimate consumer fintech app looks, to a classifier, much like a predatory one. An AI product that mentions medical or financial use cases can be sorted into those categories by a keyword. Google's healthcare policy, for example, restricts the use of prescription drug terms in ads, landing pages and keywords, so the vocabulary alone can trigger the review. A Web3 wallet is a crypto product regardless of what it holds.

Appeals exist, and sometimes succeed. They are slow, opaque and decided by the same process.

## Why legitimate companies get caught

The platform's cost of a wrong approval is high: regulatory action, press coverage, advertiser boycotts. The platform's cost of a wrong refusal is one lost small advertiser. The policy is written accordingly. Companies in reviewed categories are not being judged; they are being sorted, by a system designed to prefer refusing a legitimate business over approving a harmful one.

Regulators reinforce the asymmetry. The UK Financial Conduct Authority reported that in 2024 it had 19,766 promotions by authorised firms amended or withdrawn, interviewed 20 finfluencers under caution and issued 38 alerts against finfluencer social media accounts. A platform that carries an illegal promotion is part of that story. One that refuses a lawful one rarely is.

Recognising that is useful. It means the rejection is not personal, is not evidence the product is wrong, and is not likely to be overturned by better copy.

> Companies in reviewed categories are not being judged. They are being sorted.

## What the classification means for a distribution plan

A company that learns it is in a restricted category has learned something valuable early: which channels it cannot plan around.

The practical response is a map. For each platform and geography that matters, record whether the category is prohibited, restricted or open, what documentation a restricted approval requires, and whether the company can supply it. Then plan in three bands:

1. **Build first** in the channels that carry the category without approval: affiliate and partner programmes, creator distribution with disclosure, clipping, owned email and content, and much of programmatic.
2. **File the restricted-band paperwork** with nothing forecast against it.
3. **Write the prohibited channels down as closed,** so nobody proposes them in the next planning cycle.

The open band is usually built on partners. [Partner channel design](https://lowob.com/research/partner-channel-design/) covers how to set the roles and payment for each partner type, and [referral partners without leakage](https://lowob.com/research/referral-partners-without-leakage/) covers how to register, pay and disclose referrals. Our playbook [Meta said no](https://lowob.com/research/distribution-when-ad-platforms-restrict-you/) and the [ninety-day worked example](https://lowob.com/research/restricted-category-distribution-worked-example/) show the map in use.

## What it does not mean

It does not mean finding a way around the review. Accounts created to disguise a category, landing pages that show reviewers one thing and users another, and vendors who promise approvals are all routes to permanent bans, lost account history and, in regulated categories, worse.

Google's circumventing systems policy names cloaking, new accounts after a suspension and false information in verification programmes. It treats them as egregious: the account is suspended upon detection and without prior warning, and the advertiser cannot advertise with Google Ads again. A restricted classification is a fact about where to look for distribution. It is not a puzzle to be solved.

## lowob takeaways

- **Restricted means conditions, not refusal.** Licences, certification, geography, age and disclaimers decide it.
- **The conditions are published and dated.** Read them on the platform's own page and record the date.
- **A wrong approval costs the platform far more than a wrong refusal.** Policy is written to refuse.
- **Map, then build in the open band.** File restricted paperwork with nothing forecast against it.
- **Never disguise the category.** Cloaking and new accounts after suspension end in permanent bans.

## Common questions

### What is a restricted category in advertising?

A group of products a platform will advertise only with conditions, such as prior approval, licensing proof, certification, geographic or age limits, disclaimers or claim limits. Financial services, crypto, gambling, alcohol and health sit here on most platforms.

### Why was my legitimate fintech or crypto ad account rejected?

Platforms sort accounts by how the ad, landing page and documents look, without seeing the product in use, and a wrong approval costs them far more than a wrong refusal. The rejection is not personal and is unlikely to be overturned by better copy.

### What is the difference between a restricted and a prohibited ad category?

A restricted category can run once conditions are met, such as Google certification for a crypto exchange. A prohibited one cannot run at all, such as Google's ban on ads for DeFi trading protocols or binary options.

### Should I try to get around ad platform category restrictions?

No. Disguised accounts, landing pages that show reviewers something different, and vendors who promise approvals lead to permanent bans and, in regulated categories, worse.
